prompt: What are the two things partitioning buys, according to the lesson?
hint: Neither of them is 'every query is faster'.

choices.text: Faster inserts and smaller indexes
choices.why: Routing a row costs a little on insert, and the indexes are as big in total.

choices.text: Cheap removal of a slice, and skipping slices
choices.why: Right: the second is lesson 18's pruning, and both depend on the key.

choices.text: Unique ids across the whole table
choices.why: It is the reverse: uniqueness now has to include the partition key.

choices.text: Less WAL for every change
choices.why: Only dropping a whole partition writes little; an ordinary update writes as much as before.

prompt: How many megabytes of WAL did deleting October from the plain `events` table write?
hint: The query after the DELETE.

prompt: The `DELETE` of October ran inside a transaction that was rolled back. Had it been committed, what would still have remained to pay?
hint: Lesson 15.

choices.text: Nothing: committed rows are gone from the file
choices.why: A deleted row stays in the file as a dead version until VACUUM removes it.

choices.text: A second pass of WAL to confirm the delete
choices.why: The commit record is small; the 251 MB was already written.

choices.text: Dead rows for VACUUM, and a file that stays
choices.why: Right: 1611210 dead versions, index entries pointing at them, and space reused rather than returned.

choices.text: A rebuild of the table's primary key
choices.why: Nothing rebuilds the index; VACUUM removes its entries one by one.

prompt: Which table is the weakest candidate for partitioning?
hint: Ask how its rows leave, and what its queries filter on.

choices.text: A log of API requests kept for thirty days
choices.why: Rows arrive and leave by date; that is the case partitioning is for.

choices.text: Sensor readings, dropped after a year
choices.why: Time order in and out, and queries on a recent window: a good fit.

choices.text: Customers, read one at a time
choices.why: Right: the rows do not age and the lookups do not name a slice; an index serves them better.

choices.text: Audit events purged by month
choices.why: A monthly purge is exactly the DELETE partitioning replaces.

prompt: In `FOR VALUES FROM ('2025-10-01') TO ('2025-11-01')`, which partition does an event at `2025-11-01 00:00` go to?
hint: One of the bounds is exclusive.

choices.text: October's, because the bound includes its end
choices.why: The upper bound is not included; that is what lets months meet without overlap.

choices.text: November's
choices.why: Right: TO is exclusive, so the first instant of November is November's.

choices.text: Both, as a copy in each
choices.why: Every row lives in exactly one partition.

choices.text: It is refused as ambiguous
choices.why: The bounds are not ambiguous; overlapping ones are what the server refuses at creation.

prompt: `INSERT` of an event dated March 2026 fails with `no partition of relation "events_by_month" found for row`. What is the lasting fix?
hint: The failure arrives on a date.

choices.text: Retry the insert until it goes through
choices.why: Nothing changes between tries; there is no partition to accept it.

choices.text: Drop the partitioning and go back to one table
choices.why: That throws away what partitioning was for to fix a missing month.

choices.text: A job that creates partitions months in advance
choices.why: Right: the next month has to exist before its first row.

choices.text: Widen January's bound to the end of the year
choices.why: That makes January's partition hold a year and breaks dropping by month.

prompt: Looking up one event by `id` took one index scan on `events` and four scans on `events_by_month`. Why four?
hint: What does the id say about the month?

choices.text: The partitioned table has four copies of each row
choices.why: Each row is in exactly one partition.

choices.text: Nothing in it names the month
choices.why: Right: the condition is not on the key, so every partition has to be asked.

choices.text: The statistics on the new table were missing
choices.why: The file ran VACUUM ANALYZE; statistics do not decide which partitions a query needs.

choices.text: Lookups by id are disabled on partitioned tables
choices.why: They work; they just visit every partition.

prompt: The hidden column that says which table a row physically lives in, used to count rows per partition, is called `___`.
hint: It was cast to regclass in the count.

prompt: Which kind of partitioning gives each partition a set of named values of the key?
hint: `FOR VALUES IN (...)`.

choices.text: Range
choices.why: Range gives each partition an interval, from one value up to another.

choices.text: Hash
choices.why: Hash gives each partition a remainder; nobody names the values.

choices.text: List
choices.why: Right: as with browse and buy in the lesson.

choices.text: Default
choices.why: A default partition takes what no other accepts; it is not a kind of partitioning.

prompt: Four hash partitions by `customer_id` held about 875 thousand rows each, except one with 2372458. Why?
hint: Look at the with_customer column.

choices.text: Events without an account are all NULL, and land together
choices.why: Right: a hash spreads values, not rows, and one value was three in ten events.

choices.text: Seller 1's orders all went there
choices.why: The key was customer_id on events; sellers were not involved.

choices.text: The modulus 4 does not divide the row count evenly
choices.why: The modulus divides the hash, not the count; uneven values make uneven partitions.

choices.text: The first partition takes the overflow of the others
choices.why: There is no overflow in hashing; each row goes where its hash says.

prompt: A company keeps purchase events for five years and browsing events for ninety days. Which layout fits?
hint: Each group leaves on its own schedule.

choices.text: Hash by customer_id, to keep partitions even
choices.why: Even pieces do not help when the two groups age differently.

choices.text: No partitioning, and a DELETE per group every night
choices.why: That is the expensive removal section 02 measured.

choices.text: List partitions on the kind column, one per group
choices.why: Right: each partition is dropped or kept on its own schedule.

choices.text: One partition per customer
choices.why: Two hundred thousand partitions, and the groups still mixed inside each one.

prompt: Somebody proposes hash-partitioning `orders` by `seller_id` into eight partitions to spread the load. What should be checked first?
hint: Lesson 1 made one seller very big.

choices.text: Whether eight is a power of two
choices.why: Any modulus works; the count of partitions is not the risk here.

choices.text: Whether seller_id has an index
choices.why: Each partition gets its own index; that does not change where rows land.

choices.text: How skewed the values of the key are in the data
choices.why: Right: a quarter of the rows would land in one partition whatever the modulus.

choices.text: Whether orders has a primary key
choices.why: It has one; the question is how the rows will spread.

prompt: Removing October from `events_by_month` by DETACH and DROP wrote how much WAL, against 251 MB for the DELETE?
hint: The query after the DROP.

choices.text: 251 MB too, as the same rows were removed
choices.why: The server logged a table going away, not each row.

choices.text: 55 kB
choices.why: Right: a few records for the catalogue and the files.

choices.text: About half, because detach writes the other half later
choices.why: Nothing is written later; the 55 kB was all of it.

choices.text: Zero, since DROP is not logged
choices.why: It is logged, so replicas drop it too; it is just small.

prompt: Why add `CHECK (at >= '2026-02-01' AND at < '2026-03-01')` to a table before attaching it as February?
hint: What does the server have to be sure of?

choices.text: Without it, ATTACH refuses the table
choices.why: It attaches anyway, after reading every row to check them.

choices.text: It speeds up later inserts into February
choices.why: The partition bound already checks inserts; the constraint is about the attach.

choices.text: So the attach skips a full table scan
choices.why: Right: on a table loaded in advance that saves a full scan while the parent waits.

choices.text: It is required for the primary key
choices.why: The key needs the partition column, not a CHECK constraint.

prompt: `DETACH PARTITION events_2026_01 CONCURRENTLY` failed once the table had a partition with no interval, taking every row no other accepts. What did the error say?
hint: That partition changes what else can be done.

choices.text: That January still held rows
choices.why: January was empty; the error is about the default.

choices.text: That CONCURRENTLY needs a transaction block
choices.why: The reverse: it is not allowed inside one.

choices.text: That a default partition forbids it
choices.why: Right: `cannot detach partitions concurrently when a default partition exists`.

choices.text: That the parent was locked by another session
choices.why: Nothing else was connected; the refusal is a rule, not a wait.

prompt: Put the steps for adding next month's partition, prepared in advance, in order.
hint: The attach comes last, and it should be cheap.
items: Create the table with LIKE the parent
Load and index it while nobody can see it
Add a CHECK constraint matching the month
ATTACH PARTITION with the month's bounds
trap: Attaching before loading makes the load visible to queries; attaching without the CHECK makes the server scan every row first.

prompt: Why does `CREATE TABLE … (id bigint PRIMARY KEY, at timestamptz) PARTITION BY RANGE (at)` fail?
hint: Each partition has its own index.

choices.text: bigint cannot be a partition key
choices.why: The key here is at, and bigint could be one anyway.

choices.text: A partitioned table cannot have a primary key
choices.why: It can; events_by_month has (id, at).

choices.text: The key lacks `at`, so months cannot be compared
choices.why: Right: each partition's index only sees its own month.

choices.text: The partitions must be created first
choices.why: The parent always comes first; partitions are attached to it.

prompt: Match each statement to what happened when the lesson ran it on `events_by_month`.
hint: Two of them failed.

pairs.right: one index built on each partition

pairs.left: `PRIMARY KEY (id)` on a table partitioned by `at`
pairs.right: refused: the key lacks the partition column
the month gone, with 55 kB of WAL

prompt: Which of these are true of indexes on `events_by_month`? Choose all that apply.
hint: An index on the parent is many indexes.

choices.text: Dropping a month drops its indexes with it
choices.why: Right: they belong to the partition's table.

choices.text: A REINDEX can be done one month at a time
choices.why: Right: each partition's index is its own.

choices.text: ATTACH builds a missing matching index on the table being attached
choices.why: Right: and on a big table that is slow, so build it before.

choices.text: One index on the parent covers every month in a single tree
choices.why: There is one tree per partition; that is why uniqueness needs the key.

choices.text: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY works on the parent
choices.why: It was refused; the way round is ON ONLY plus each partition.

prompt: A nightly `DELETE … WHERE created_at < now() - interval '90 days'` on a 400 GB log table now runs for an hour and the replicas fall behind while it does. Which change attacks the cause?
hint: What do the replicas have to receive?

choices.text: Run the DELETE every hour instead of every night
choices.why: Smaller batches spread the cost but write the same WAL and dead rows in total.

choices.text: Partition by day; drop old days
choices.why: Right: dropping writes kilobytes of WAL and leaves nothing for VACUUM.

choices.text: Add an index on created_at
choices.why: It finds the rows faster but the deletion still writes every row to the WAL.

choices.text: Hash-partition by request id into sixteen pieces
choices.why: Old rows would be spread across all sixteen, so each still needs a DELETE.

prompt: Which statement about partitioning does the lesson support?
hint: Think of the id lookup.

choices.text: Not naming the key costs more work
choices.why: Right: the id lookup did four scans instead of one, and planned for longer.

choices.text: A partitioned table answers every query at least as fast
choices.why: The id lookup was slower in planning and execution.

choices.text: A default partition is needed for the table to accept inserts
choices.why: Inserts into existing months worked without one.

choices.text: Hash partitioning keeps partitions equal in rows
choices.why: The NULLs made one partition nearly three times the others.
